lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.unitTitle: Decision Analysis and Expected Value Capstone
lessonRef.title: Reteach and varied practice: expected payoff of a decision

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: These two examples show the same idea in two different formats.

items.prompt: A has expected payoff $12, B has $9. Which, and what is ignored?

steps: A has the higher expected value.
Spread and risk tolerance are not captured.

items.prompt: Is a die with faces split 3/2/1 among three people fair?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A game costs $4 to play. It pays $45 with probability 1/5 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
choices: $5; the game is favourable to the player
$-4; the game is unfavourable to the player
$41; the game is favourable to the player
$9; the game is favourable to the player

items.prompt: An insurer charges a premium of $8 and pays out $93 with probability 1/31. Find the insurer's expected profit per policy.
Option A has expected payoff $8 and Option B has expected payoff $25. On expected value alone, which should be chosen, and what does this criterion ignore?
choices: Option B; expected value already accounts for risk, so nothing is ignored.
Option A; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Neither; expected value cannot compare two options.
Option B; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between three people by rolling a standard die, assigning faces 1–3, 4–5, and 6.
choices: Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.
Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.
Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.
Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A game costs $4 to play. It pays $60 with probability 1/10 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
choices: $-4; the game is unfavourable to the player
$6; the game is favourable to the player
$56; the game is favourable to the player
$2; the game is favourable to the player

items.prompt: An insurer charges a premium of $16 and pays out $170 with probability 1/85. Find the insurer's expected profit per policy.
Option A has expected payoff $7 and Option B has expected payoff $28. On expected value alone, which should be chosen, and what does this criterion ignore?
choices: Option A; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Option B; expected value already accounts for risk, so nothing is ignored.
Option B; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Neither; expected value cannot compare two options.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between two people using a single fair coin flip.
choices: Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.
Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.
Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.
Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.

items.prompt: A game costs $10 to play. It pays $150 with probability 1/10 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
choices: $15; the game is favourable to the player
$140; the game is favourable to the player
$5; the game is favourable to the player
$-10; the game is unfavourable to the player
